title: Cerulean Health - POC scoping (latency SLOs)
summary: POC scoping for latency and throughput SLOs. Discussed success criteria (TTFT vs TPOT), target p95/p99 thresholds, representative workload sizing, benchmark plan and timeline. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmark harness and initial config; customer to provide sample prompts and traffic profile; run baseline by week of 12/21.
topics: TTFT vs TPOT definitions and targets
next_steps: Jordan to share benchmark harness + runbook (by 2026-12-20)
Cerulean to share sample prompts, token distribution and production QPS (by 2026-12-20)
Schedule baseline hosted run and private run week of 2026-12-21
Maya to define measurement dashboards and Prometheus/Histogram metrics config
action_items: Jordan: send benchmark harness and sample config by 2026-12-20
Priya: export 7-day sample of prompts + token histogram by 2026-12-20
Maya: prepare Prometheus histogram and Grafana dashboard template by 2026-12-21
Samir: confirm networking constraints for private VPC test by 2026-12-22
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll focus on latency and throughput SLOs for the POC. we want to make sure we're aligned on success criteria and how we measure. i know you sent over the runbook notes, thanks.
[00:12] Ethan (Customer): yeah thanks, uh we also want to confirm the difference between TTFT and TPOT cause our infra folks keep asking.
[00:18] Maya (Redwood): sure, quick shorthand: TTFT is time-to-first-token, that's the latency before the first token is emitted. TPOT we use as time-per-token (sometimes folks say per-token latency) which matters for longer responses. both matter depending on UX.
[00:33] Priya (Customer): okay that helps, so for our chat use case TTFT is more important for snappy responses, but for report-gen the TPOT matters.
[00:40] Jordan: exactly. for the POC let's define SLOs at p95 and p99 for both. any initial targets you think are must-haves?
[00:47] Ethan: our internal bar is p95 TTFT < 200ms and p99 < 400ms for chat. for longer responses we want time-per-token p95 < 25ms p99 < 60ms, but that's flexible.
[01:02] Maya: those are helpful starting points. two quick clarifications: 1) are those targets under steady-state traffic or under load? and 2) what's the acceptable error/retry budget?
[01:14] Samir: good Q — we want them met under 80% of expected peak QPS, errors less than 1% and tail latencies not spiking > 2x. network jitter tolerated but we want consistent performance.
[01:26] Jordan: ok so SLO framing: p95 TTFT <= 200ms, p99 TTFT <= 400ms for chat flows; TPOT p95 <= 25ms, p99 <= 60ms for generation flows. error rate <=1% and targets should hold at 80% of peak QPS. we'll record that as acceptance criteria.
[01:40] Priya: makes sense. now for workload sizing — our peak QPS is around 120 rps for chat and 30 rps for generation during business hours. token distribution: median response ~32 tokens, 95th ~220 tokens.
[01:56] Maya: great, that's actionable. for benchmarking we recommend three tiers: baseline (single model instance, cold start), steady-state warm (cached KV/prefix hit rates), and load test at 80% and 100% peak.
[02:09] Jordan: also important — measure both hosted Redwood environment and our private VPC setup. some customers see different TTFT due to network egress and private infra.
[02:18] Ethan: our security folks want to see SOC2 + KMS integration for private. we'll sign NDAs but need measurement in our VPC.
[02:25] Maya: noted — we'll bring the private-run playbook. measurement plan details:
[02:29] Maya: 1) use the benchmark harness (we'll share) that replays a sampled workload of your prompts, preserving token counts and timestamps. 2) run 3x warm runs (after prefix/KV cache primed) and 3x cold runs. 3) collect per-request TTFT and per-token latencies, store histograms (prometheus histogram buckets), and compute p50/p95/p99.
[02:49] Samir: can you show how you capture TPOT? i've seen differing definitions in other tools.
[02:53] Maya: we measure TPOT as the average inter-token emission time once generation starts, and also aggregate per-request average tokens/sec. practical metric is ms/token; we'll report p95/p99 ms/token and tokens/sec at throughput.
[03:05] Priya: what about batching and continuous batching effects? that can lower cost but change TTFT.
[03:09] Jordan: yes tradeoff: aggressive batching reduces cost and increases overall throughput, but can add to TTFT for low-latency chat. as part of the POC we'll test a few configurations: minimal batching (low-latency), moderate batching (balance), and cost-optimized batching (higher TTFT but lower cost).
[03:26] Ethan: can you put numbers on batching? like how much does 2-10ms get added?
[03:29] Maya: depends on queue windows. small window batching can add ~5-30ms to TTFT but can reduce per-token cost by 10-40%. we'll include that in the benchmark matrix.
[03:39] Jordan: measurement plan also covers warm caches — we need to simulate realistic prefix cache hit rates. Priya you mentioned many repeated prompts in chat?
[03:47] Priya: yes around 20% of prompts are repeated templates where caching helps.
[03:51] Maya: ok we'll set prefix/KV cache hit rates at 0%, 20%, 60% for tests.
[03:56] Ethan: good. timeline — when can we get first pass?
[03:59] Jordan: we can share benchmark harness and runbook by Mon 2026-12-20. if you provide sample prompts and QPS profile same day we can schedule baseline hosted run Tues/Wed and private run Thurs/Fri pending networking. goal to have results and deck by week of 12/28.
[04:17] Samir: for private we may need a small firewall rule; i'll check with infra and confirm by 12/22.
[04:22] Priya: what's the sample size for runs? we need statistical significance.
[04:25] Maya: we'll do at least 10k requests for steady-state runs and 1k for cold starts, and ensure 99% CI on p95 using bootstrapping. we'll also produce request-level logs and a CSV with per-request TTFT and per-token timings.
[04:43] Ethan: perfect. any thoughts on acceptance beyond latency? e.g., quality regressions or mismatch in outputs between model variants?
[04:50] Jordan: yes we'll tie quality checks to a small eval suite you provide. the POC acceptance requires no meaningful drop in quality — we'll compare embeddings/ROUGE/semantic similarity on a set. if quality drops >2% on your metrics, it's a failure even if latency's good.
[05:03] Priya: ok that seems fair.
[05:06] Jordan: quick note on monitoring — we'll provide a Grafana dashboard template with p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, error rates, and tokens/sec, and alerting thresholds. Maya will send the dashboard JSON.
[05:18] Maya: i'll include Prometheus histogram config and example alerts (p99 TTFT > 400ms for >5m).
[05:24] Ethan: competitors — we compared to Vertex last month; their cold TTFT was okay but tail worse. Anthropic was costly for our token volumes. will want to include cost per 1k tokens in evaluation.
[05:34] Jordan: we'll include a cost breakdown (tokens, GPU hours, orchestration) for each configuration in the deck.
[05:40] Priya: one more ops constraint: our SRE prefers deployments that support canary rollouts and automatic fallback to smaller model variants on overload. do you support that?
[05:48] Maya: yes Redwood has model routing and automatic fallbacks; we'll demo canary rollouts in a follow-up demo if you want.
[05:55] Jordan: wrap up and recap next steps. action items we've captured: Jordan sends harness/runbook, Maya sends dashboards and prometheus config, Priya shares prompts and token histogram, Samir checks firewall. baseline hosted run slated 12/21-12/22, private run 12/23-12/24 if infra ready. results and deck week of 12/28.
[06:18] Ethan: thanks everyone, that timeline works.
[06:20] Jordan: great thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the runs and share the repo link in the notes.
[06:26] (end)
notes: Will compare hosted vs private VPC runs
